svg.aria-label: Diagram: what an AWS Resource Access Manager resource share confers on a consuming account, how that differs from achieving apparently the same thing with a resource-based policy, and what happens when the share is deleted. AWS states that when you share a resource in the owning account with another AWS account, the consuming account, you are granting access for principals in the consuming account to the shared resource, and that any policies and permissions that apply to roles and users in the consuming account also apply to the shared resource. So two independent permission decisions must agree: the owner decides which principals the share names, and the consuming account's own IAM decides which of its roles and users may act on the resource, and those two decisions sit in different change-control processes. Principals can be individual AWS accounts, the accounts in an organization or an organizational unit in AWS Organizations, or individual IAM roles or users, but AWS notes that not all resource types can be shared with IAM roles and users, so for many resource types the finest granularity available to the owner is the account. The owner is not blind, since owners of a resource can see which principals have access to each individual resource they have shared, but what the owner sees is the principal the share names rather than the identity that ultimately uses the resource. The resources in a share look like they are native resources in the AWS accounts they are shared with, which removes real friction and also means nothing in the normal console view distinguishes a resource the account owns from one it has been lent. Comparing the two mechanisms: a resource-based policy can also share some types of resources with other accounts by identifying IAM principals outside the owning account, but AWS states that sharing by attaching a policy does not take advantage of the additional benefits RAM provides. The differences are that RAM lets you share with an organization or organizational unit without having to enumerate every one of the AWS account IDs; that with RAM users can see the resources shared with them directly in the originating service console and API operations as if those resources were directly in the user's account, with AWS's example being a shared VPC subnet appearing in the Amazon VPC console and in the results of VPC API operations performed in that account; and that resources shared by attaching a resource-based policy are not visible that way, so you have to discover and explicitly refer to the resource by its Amazon Resource Name. A resource-policy share is therefore access nobody can find by looking, working for the team that was told the ARN and invisible to the next engineer taking inventory from the consuming side. Resources already shared by a resource-based permission policy can be promoted to fully RAM managed resources using the PromoteResourceShareCreatedFromPolicy API operation or the equivalent promote-resource-share-created-from-policy CLI command, whose name indicates that a policy share produces something RAM already models in a not-fully-managed state, which in turn means an inventory of RAM shares and an inventory of cross-account access are not the same list. On acceptance, sharing with an account that is not part of your organization causes RAM to initiate an invitation process and the recipient must accept the invitation before that principal can access the shared resources, whereas after turning on the ability to share within your organization, sharing with accounts in the organization does not require invitations, which means the same API call produces a pending invitation in one case and immediate live access in the other depending on organization membership, so a share that appears not to have worked may be a share awaiting acceptance. Within the owning account, RAM simplifies granting access to every role and user in that account without having to use identity-based permission policies, so the mechanism's natural grain is everyone in the account and narrowing it is work added rather than removed. On deletion, when you delete a resource share all principals that were associated with the resource share lose access to the shared resources, but deleting a resource share does not delete the shared resources, which is the correct separation because revocation that destroyed data would be an operation nobody would dare perform. AWS warns that you cannot recover a resource share after you delete it, so the resource survives while the share, its principal list and its permissions do not, making a scripted share recoverable from source even though it is not recoverable from the API. A deleted resource share disappears after two hours and until then remains visible in the console with a deleted status, so during that window the console shows an object that no longer does anything and an automation polling for the share's absence to confirm revocation will wait two hours for a state change that was already complete; revocation should be confirmed by checking the status field or from the consuming side instead. If you need to delete an AWS resource that you included in a resource share, AWS recommends first ensuring that you either remove the resource from any resource share that includes it, or delete the resource share. On Region scoping, a resource share can contain only Regional resources that are in the same AWS Region as the resource share, and can contain global resources only if the resource share is in the designated home Region for global resources, US East Northern Virginia, us-east-1; because resource shares exist in specific Regions, to see shares containing global resources in the console you must set the Region to us-east-1, which means a share can appear to be missing simply because the console is pointed at the wrong Region.
svg.title: The owner names the principal; the consuming account's IAM decides who acts
svg.text: A share is a grant to an account. The account grants to the person.
AWS Resource Access Manager — what a share confers, and who administers the other half of it.
The sentence that is easy to read past
“you are granting access for principals in the consuming account to the shared resource. Any policies and
permissions that apply to roles and users in the consuming account also apply to the shared resource.”
Decision 1 — the OWNER
Which principals the share names: an account, an
organization or OU, or IAM roles and users — but
“Not all resource types can be shared with
IAM roles and users.”
So for many types the finest grain is the account.
Decision 2 — the CONSUMING ACCOUNT
Which of its roles and users may act, via its own IAM.
Authored in somebody else’s change control.
The owner is not blind — owners “can see which principals
have access” — but that is the principal the share names,
not the identity that ends up using it.
AND
And it looks like it was always theirs
“The resources in the share look like they’re native resources in the AWS accounts you shared them with.” Best
thing about RAM, and the thing most likely to mislead: nothing in the normal view says “this is on loan”.
RAM share
· share to an org or OU “without having to
enumerate every one of the AWS account IDs”
· visible “in the originating AWS service console”
— a shared subnet appears in the VPC console
· owner sees the principals
· invitation workflow outside the organization
Resource-based policy
Grants the same access. But:
“aren’t visible this way; instead, you have to
discover and explicitly refer to the resource by
its Amazon Resource Name (ARN)”
Access nobody can find by looking. Works for whoever
was told the ARN; invisible to their successor.
The API name gives the game away: PromoteResourceShareCreatedFromPolicy
A policy share is already something RAM models, un-managed. So “list my RAM shares” and “list my cross-account access” are two inventories.
Deleting the share
“all principals… lose access to the shared resources”
“Deleting a resource share doesn’t delete
the shared resources.” — the right separation
“You can’t recover a resource share after you
delete it.” → keep share definitions in code
The two-hour observability trap
“The deleted resource share disappears after two
hours. Until then, it remains visible in the console
with a deleted status.”
Access ends at once; the row lingers. Polling for the row to
vanish waits 2h for a change already complete. Read status.
Region scoping: a share holds only Regional resources from its own Region, and holds global resources only in us-east-1.
To see a global-resource share you must also be in us-east-1 — so a share can look missing because the console points elsewhere.
Same class as everything in this block: an absent row reads as “no such thing” when it means “not in this view”.
